newsitem.title: ITALY: Turkey's Ciller says Europe has rights problem too.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Ciller says Europe has rights problem too.

text.p: Turkey is working on its human rights record but Europe should acknowledge that it also has a problem, Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said on Thursday.
"The issue is not just for Turkey but it is for the whole of Europe. We also feel that there are many cases in Europe which are violations of human rights which should be corrected," Ciller said.
"If it is needed I can (list) them but at this point in time that's all I want to say," she said.
Ciller spoke to reporters after talks with Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini at which they discussed Turkey's bid to become a full member of the European Union.
Dini acknowledged that civil rights, human rights and the democratisation process were still issues affecting Turkey's membership bid.
But he said the EU was not trying to place any "new conditions" on Turkey and that dialogue between Europe and Ankara aimed at membership had to continue.
The two met as the U.S. State Department said in its annual human rights report that Turkey had serious problems in 1996 and that its record deteriorated in some respects.
It was not clear if Ciller or Dini were aware of the report when they made their comments.

"The issue of human rights in Turkey is not a condition for the European Union," Ciller said. "It is a condition for our own people because we feel that human rights is something needed by our own people."
She said reform was a continuous process and "not just a one-shot".

The State Department report said the Turkish government "was unable to sustain improvements made in 1995 and, as a result, its record was uneven in 1996 and deteriorated in some respects...Serious human rights problems continued."

The report said of "particular concern" was the situation in southeast Turkey, where the government "has long denied its Kurdish population, located largely in the southeast, basic cultural and linguistic rights."
Dini said Italy had encouraged Ciller to continue dialogue to resolve the Kurdish question.

Also, the United States charged that "extrajudicial killings, including deaths in detention, from the excessive use of force, in safe house raids, and mystery killings continued to occur with disturbing frequency."
Ciller insisted that Ankara was moving forward on human rights.

"Our commitment to furthering and increasing the standards of our democracy and moving ahead in the human rights arena...is something that is needed by our own people and that's why we will carry the flag for that further," she said.

Ciller repeated Ankara's frustration over what it considers a second-rate relationship with the EU after nearly half a century as a NATO member which help defend the West from communism before the collapse of the Berlin Wall.
"Now is celebration time and it is only fair to expect that we will share it all together with all the allies and with all those for whom we have fought," she said.
